candidates.attacker_control: A party able to publish a message to the RabbitMQ exchange/queue consumed by a Camel `rabbitmq:` route controls (a) the AMQP basic-properties header map and (b) the binary body. Setting the header key `CamelSerialize` (RabbitMQEndpoint.SERIALIZE_HEADER, RabbitMQEndpoint.java:58) to a Boolean true value routes the body into deserializeBody(); the body bytes are then read directly into ObjectInputStream.readObject(). No signature, sender identity check, or per-message opt-out is applied (the header is only removed from headers later by mergeAmqpProperties/header population, not from the properties used for the decision).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The deserialization is gated by `CamelSerialize` and is used deliberately for Camel-to-Camel object transfer (RabbitMQMessagePublisher.java:87-93 sets it when the body is Serializable), so in a fully closed system the path is intentional; however the gate value is entirely sender-controlled, so any producer can opt the consumer into Java deserialization — it is not a security control. `transferException`/`allowNullHeaders` on the endpoint do not affect this path (grep-verified). By contrast, other Camel components in the same snapshot gate Java deserialization behind explicit options that default to false (camel-http-common/DefaultHttpBinding.java:199-206, camel-ahc/DefaultAhcBinding.java:284-288, camel-jms `allowSerializedHeaders`), showing the missing opt-out here is an inconsistency rather than an inherent requirement. I found no allow-list, class-resolver restriction, or configuration flag anywhere in camel-rabbitmq (repository-wide searches for allowJavaSerializedMessage/trustedPackages/serialization restrictions returned nothing).
candidates.impact: Remote code execution in the Camel consumer JVM via deserialization of a malicious Java object stream (gadget-chain dependent), or at minimum arbitrary class loading/instantiation and denial of service. The trust boundary is the AMQP broker/exchange: a producer that would normally only be able to deliver data obtains code-execution influence over the consumer process.
candidates.prerequisites: A Camel route consuming from the rabbitmq component (or the reply-manager path) is deployed, and the attacker can publish/route a message to that exchange/queue (broker credentials, an unauthenticated broker/vhost, a shared exchange, or a compromised producer). The `CamelSerialize` header must be sent as an AMQP boolean true. Exploitation to code execution additionally requires a usable gadget chain on the consumer JVM classpath; absent that, arbitrary object instantiation/exception paths still give a denial-of-service/instability primitive.
candidates.root_cause: RabbitMQMessageConverter.populateMessageBody() unconditionally calls deserializeBody() when the incoming AMQP message carries the header CamelSerialize=true, and deserializeBody() performs `new ObjectInputStream(byteArrayInputStream).readObject()` on the raw broker delivery body. The trigger flag is part of the message properties supplied by whichever client published the message, and this snapshot exposes no endpoint/component option to disable Java deserialization or restrict the classes that may be instantiated (no allowJavaSerializedMessage / trustedPackages-style guard; verified absent by repository-wide search). The consumer therefore treats an untrusted broker publisher as authoritative for a Java-deserialization decision.
candidates.title: camel-rabbitmq consumer deserializes sender-controlled Java object bodies without any allow-list/opt-out (CWE-502)
candidates.trace: RabbitConsumer.doHandleDelivery(consumerTag, envelope, properties, body) (RabbitConsumer.java:93) -> RabbitMQEndpoint.createRabbitExchange(envelope, properties, body) (RabbitMQEndpoint.java:192-195) -> RabbitMQMessageConverter.populateRabbitExchange(...) (RabbitMQMessageConverter.java:236-240) -> populateMessageBody(message, camelExchange, properties, body) (287-294) -> hasSerializeHeader(properties) (313-315) -> isSerializeHeaderEnabled(properties) reads properties.getHeaders().get("CamelSerialize") (321-323) -> deserializeBody(...) (296-311) -> `new ObjectInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(body)).readObject()` (300).
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed and no exploit executed. Broker authorisation model is deployment-specific (the prerequisite is publish access or an unauthenticated broker). Gadget availability on the consumer classpath is unproven. I could not diff against upstream to confirm this is the specific change the snapshot was built around; the finding is based on the source-visible missing guard, and the relation index (which flags this exact readObject location as a deserialization hint) is navigation-only evidence.

coverage_summary: Source scope per get_source_scope: 8,585 model-visible files (8,588 source-root files; 0 binaries counted, 3 files excluded by sensitive-name/path filter) with the same filters applied to B0/P1. Relation scope per get_relation_scope: index complete over 8,588 files, 0 files missing/hash-mismatched, but it is syntactic navigation only (218,954 call edges, 2,153 heuristic facts; no data-flow, reachability, or exploitability proof; build/tests not run). I inspected the repository layout and modules, enumerated Java-deserialization sinks by text search and by the index's `deserialization` security-call facts, traced the RabbitMQ consumer path end-to-end in source, examined the other gated Java-serialization paths (camel-http-common, camel-http, camel-ahc, camel-jetty, camel-jms, camel-netty/netty-http), checked path-traversal/jail handling in camel-file, camel-tarfile and camel-zipfile, checked camel-shiro token handling, camel-elytron authorization, camel-ldif URL fetch, JMX connector creation, and sampled SQL/weka/undertow handling. Not inspected in any depth: the majority of the ~300 components, most of `tooling/`, `catalog/`, `platforms/`, generated endpoint-DSL factories (spot-checked only), and any build/test execution.
limitations: Static review only: no code was executed, no tests or scanners were run, and no runtime behavior or exploitability was confirmed.
No upstream/GitHub comparison is available in this run, so I could not diff the snapshot against the upstream 3.1.0 tree to confirm which specific security fix this snapshot precedes.
The source snapshot contains almost no test or documentation files, so regression tests and advisory text that might identify the intended fix are unavailable.
The P1 relation index has no record of implicit deserialization sinks (e.g. the Netty ObjectDecoder installed by NettyConfiguration), so absence of an index hint is not evidence of absence.
The RabbitMQ finding requires broker publish access and a classpath gadget chain; neither could be verified here, and the endpoint/component option set was checked only for this snapshot.

Broker/elicitation semantics of the `CamelSerialize` header (typed Boolean true versus string "true") were derived from source (`Boolean.TRUE.equals(...)`) plus the publisher code; not runtime-verified.

rejected_leads.lead: camel-netty default codec: NettyConfiguration.setup() installs Netty ObjectEncoder/ObjectDecoder by default when textline=false and no codec is configured (components/camel-netty/src/main/java/org/apache/camel/component/netty/NettyConfiguration.java:206-233, ChannelHandlerFactories.java:67-81), i.e. Java deserialization from any unauthenticated network peer on a `netty:tcp://` consumer.
rejected_leads.reason: Strong impact, but the object codec is long-standing documented behavior with explicit mitigations (`allowDefaultCodec=false`, `textline=true`), the sink lives inside Netty's ObjectDecoder rather than Camel code (no readObject call to evidence), the relation index contains no hint for it, and I could not confirm from source that this snapshot's intended vulnerable change is here. Kept out of the candidate slot as the weaker/more uncertain of the two deserialization leads.

rejected_leads.lead: camel-elytron role-check bypass: ElytronConsumer.handleRequest()/isAllowed() (components/camel-elytron/.../ElytronConsumer.java:48-83) forwards the request to the Camel route without any allowedRoles check when SecurityDomain.getCurrentSecurityIdentity() is null, and ElytronEndpoint.allowedRolesList defaults to an empty list.
rejected_leads.reason: Potentially an authorization bypass, but reachability of the null-identity branch depends on the configured Elytron HTTP mechanism/security-domain (some mechanisms challenge and reject anonymous requests before this handler), and the component is brand new in 3.1.0 with no proof the branch is attacker-reachable.

rejected_leads.lead: camel-ldif producer fetches a URL taken from the message body: LdifProducer.process() (components/camel-ldif/.../LdifProducer.java:66-91) does `new URL(body).openStream()` for non-LDIF string bodies (SSRF / local file read via file:, jar:, etc.).
rejected_leads.reason: Real sink, but it is the component's documented purpose (body may be LDIF text or a URL) and requires an attacker-influenced exchange reaching an ldif producer route; comparatively weak trust-boundary story.

rejected_leads.lead: Aggregation repositories deserialize Java state: camel-sql JdbcCamelCodec (components/camel-sql/.../JdbcCamelCodec.java:94-98), camel-cassandraql CassandraCamelCodec:82-86, camel-hbase HBaseHelper:104-108, camel-consul ConsulRegistry:273-279.
rejected_leads.reason: All read back state written by the same application/repository; an attacker would need write access to the backing SQL/Cassandra/HBase/Consul store first, a materially weaker precondition than the broker/network-facing paths.
Rejected: the serialized token is decrypted with the configured Shiro passphrase/cipher before readObject(), so an attacker without the passphrase cannot inject a crafted stream.

summary: Reviewed the Apache Camel 3.1.0-SNAPSHOT source snapshot (8,585 visible source files; build/test/doc artifacts largely absent) as a static, defensive assessment. After tracing deserialization sinks (via grep and the P1 relation index), path-handling checks, serialization gates, and HTTP/auth components, the strongest source-evidenced issue is that the camel-rabbitmq consumer deserializes attacker-crafted AMQP message bodies with plain Java `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` whenever the *sender-controlled* AMQP header `CamelSerialize=true` is present, with no allow-list or opt-out in this snapshot. Other plausible-but-weaker leads (netty's implicit default object codec, an elytron null-identity role-check bypass, LDIF body-controlled URL fetch, datastore-driven aggregation-repository deserialization) are listed as rejected/unconfirmed leads rather than additional candidates.
